messages.subject: Fix for non-convergence
parts:
Hi, I am hoping to get some advice on how to fix models that don't converge. 

I have point transect camera trap data, with 973 obervations from 45 cameras (input data attached). Plotting the inital data suggests truncating at: L= 1.5 R=6m. After going through the model selection process (based on QAIC and c-hat values), hr0 is the chosen model. 

When I run the bootstrap for variance estimation, the model works for 99 bootstraps but for 999 bootstarps I get the following errors:
ng in ddf.ds(model = dsmodel, data, meta.data = meta.data, control = control, : Estimated hazard-rate scale parameter close to 0 (on log scale). Possible problem in data (e.g., spike near zero distance). 

Warning in ddf.ds(model = dsmodel, data, meta.data = meta.data, control = control, : Model fitting did not converge. Try different initial values or different model

I can see that the probem is likely arising from the spikes I have in my data around 2 and 2.5m. 

I have tried alternative models and differnt L truncation distances but still always have the second of these two errors. 

Is the best approach to try changing the start values using the 'start' argument? I am confused as to how this works i.e. how you know what values to set this to? And is it used within the ds function, so would I add it in here?

hr0 <- ds(wicca.data, transect = "point", key="hr", adjustment = NULL,
          convert_units = conversion.factor,
          truncation = trunc.list)

Also, if this is the thing to try, should I add the same start values to all of the potential models before model selection or just use the start argument for the chosen model?

I have attached plots of the inital model fitting and chosen model.

Would be grateful for any advice.

Many thanks,

Verity

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Fix for non-convergence
parts:
Verity

Welcome to the world of convergence failure in models. This can easily happen when bootstrapping. As you saw, you were "lucky" with your 99 resamples—they all behaved reasonably, but when you boosted the number of replicates, your luck ran out. If the distribution of detection distances vary widely between cameras (as you mentioned in the case of those near dens and those far from dens) resampling the camera stations can produce distributions of detection distances that give problems to the model fitting algorithms.

We spoke about overdispersion in camera trap data during our workshop; that adds to the problem of model fitting. Hence, there are two problems working against you—bootstraps and overdispersion.

You have two choices: read the documentation found in ?mrds::mrds-opt​ offering suggestions about model fitting in awkward situations such as yours. That is where the topic of specifying starting values is raised.

I learned how to provide starting values to the ds​ function, using the Duiker camera trap data set as an example and the hazard rate without adjustments. I fit the model and harvest the parameter estimates from the successful fit, then place those estimates into the argument initial_values​ for another fit. Printing the number of fitting iterations of the first fit and the second fit, I see providing starting values resulted in fewer iterations to find a solution.

library(Distance)
data("DuikerCameraTraps")
trunc.list <- list(left=2, right=15)
mybreaks <- c(seq(2,8,1), 10, 12, 15)
conversion <- convert_units("meter", NULL, "square kilometer")
hr0 <- ds(DuikerCameraTraps, transect = "point", key="hr",
          adjustment = NULL,
          convert_units = conversion,
           cutpoints = mybreaks, truncation = trunc.list)

params <- unname(hr0$ddf$par)
par.correct.order <- rev(params)

hrrefit <- ds(DuikerCameraTraps, transect = "point", key="hr",
              adjustment = NULL,
              convert_units = conversion,
              cutpoints = mybreaks, truncation = trunc.list,
              initial_values = list(scale=par.correct.order[1],
                                    shape=par.correct.order[2]))
print(hr0$ddf$ds$niter)
print(hrrefit$ddf$ds$niter)

This is all fine for a single call to ds​. What I do not know is whether these starting values provided to ds​ are passed along to bootdht​ when it is performing the bootstrapping. You might report back your findings.

I said there were two choices. The second choice is to perform your bootstrapping analysis using the Distance for Windows software. It was enhanced a year ago to "understand" camera trapping data. The optimisation engine in that software has been highly tuned for detection function model fitting; I predict that the probability of convergence failures will be smaller if you do your bootstrapping with Distance for Windows.

My colleagues are more astute fitters of CTDS data, they may have further suggestions.
